title: Open Superconductor Challenge: Help Discover the Next 2D Superconductor — From Your Laptop
gist: FINAL-Bench's Open Superconductor Challenge on Hugging Face crowdsources laptop-CPU screening of 2D materials for d-wave superconductivity, reserving expensive many-body verification for top submissions ('compute arbitrage'), with a $3,000 prize pool, co-authorship and AI-agent participation; 63 of a 4,832-material universe currently have effective models and CuS2 leads the verified board.

insights.claim: The Open Superconductor Challenge splits superconductor discovery into cheap crowd screening on laptop CPUs and expensive precise many-body verification run by organizers only on top submissions, a model the hosts call 'compute arbitrage'.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Shows a template for cutting scientific-discovery compute cost by tiering cheap distributed screening ahead of costly verification.
insights.quote: This "compute arbitrage" finds promising superconductor candidates for a fraction of the usual cost
insights.locator: The idea: crowd-screen first, verify precisely

insights.claim: Experimental discovery of new superconducting materials is slow because each candidate can take months in the lab while thousands of promising 2D materials remain to be checked, motivating computational pre-screening.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Computational screening that shortens lab cycles addresses a core bottleneck in materials R&D timelines.
insights.quote: each candidate can take months in the lab, and there are thousands of promising 2D materials to check
insights.locator: The problem: finding superconductors is slow

insights.claim: Everything participants need is open, while only the final verification engine stays private to keep the leaderboard fair and hard to game.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Partially-closed verification is a design pattern for open benchmarks resisting gaming.
insights.quote: Only the final verification engine stays private, which keeps the leaderboard fair and hard to game without hiding the science.

insights.claim: Participants receive a downfolded doped Hubbard effective model per material, with the correlated regime fixed at U/t = 8, and must produce a material-specific d-wave pairing estimate that beats the first-order density-of-states screen.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Standardized effective models lower the barrier for ML and non-specialist participation in condensed-matter problems.
insights.quote: the challenge fixes the correlated regime at U/t = 8
insights.locator: What you get, and what you do

insights.claim: The OSC active set has computed effective models for 63 materials out of a 4,832-material universe, and the set is described as growing.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Indicates the early stage and coverage of the screening effort.
insights.quote: a computed effective model for 63 materials out of a 4,832-material universe

insights.claim: Materials in the challenge derive from the Computational 2D Materials Database (C2DB) under a CC-BY 4.0 license, enriched by the organizers.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Open-licensed public materials data underpins community AI-for-science efforts.

insights.claim: The entry path requires no GPU or installation: a single pure-Python instrument runs in seconds on a laptop, while gold-track competitors can swap in ED, VMC, DMRG, mean-field or ML methods.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Low hardware barriers broaden the contributor pool for scientific crowdsourcing.

insights.claim: AI coding agents such as Claude Code or Codex are explicitly invited to claim a material, run the instrument and submit results autonomously.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Signals AI agents being treated as first-class participants in scientific research workflows.
insights.quote: point Claude Code or Codex at the challenge and it can claim a material, run the instrument, and submit for you.

insights.claim: The current verified top five by OSC Pairing Index are CuS2 (23.31), NV2 (20.39), Co2Se2 (16.82), H2Ti (16.21) and Br2Cu (15.86).
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Names the leading computational superconductor candidates flagged for further study.

insights.claim: The OSC Pairing Index equals N(E_F) x A_ref x 10000, with A_ref = 0.0503 from a 6x6 doped-Hubbard reference solver, and a higher index indicates a stronger d-wave pairing tendency rather than a guaranteed critical temperature.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Investors should not read leaderboard leaders as confirmed superconductors; it is a first-order screen.
insights.quote: A higher index means a stronger d-wave pairing tendency by our screen — a better candidate to investigate — not a guaranteed critical temperature.

insights.claim: The organizers state that the top-ranked material is not a confirmed superconductor but only the strongest d-wave candidate by the first-order screen, with no measured Tc.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Tempers any hype around 'discovered' superconductors from computational leaderboards.
insights.quote: it is the strongest d-wave candidate by our first-order screen, not a measured Tc.

insights.claim: The challenge offers a US$3,000 prize pool split into $1,500 grand, $1,000 best open-sourced method and $500 best new material discovery, plus co-authorship for ranks 2-5 and all valid entrants; Season 1 closes 31 December 2026.
insights.speaker: VIDRAFT_LAB
insights.so_what: Small cash plus co-authorship incentives show the low-cost economics of crowdsourced science.
